newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's new labour bill passed in parliament.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's new labour bill passed in parliament.

text.p: South Korea's parliament passed a new labour bill on Monday, replacing a law that sparked almost one month of labour strikes.
In a night session of the National Assembly, parliamentary speaker Kim Soo-han banged his gavel to adopt the bill after 192 members of parliament stood up to signal their support.
Ten opposed the bill.
"Labour and management should cooperate to lay a fresh foundation of national construction," Kim said.

The ruling New Korea Party, bowing to pressure from home and abroad, agreed in the revised legislation to delay for two years implementation of a controversial clause making it easier for companies to lay off workers.
Layoffs have been all but impossible in South Korea, where redundancies must be approved by a court.

Provisions designed to discourage strikes that have plagued the economy were watered down and instant recognition was offered to the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which spearheaded industrial action after the law was rammed through parliament on December 26.
But the confederation immediately denounced the new legislation and vowed to organise fresh protests.
"There's no big difference between the original bill and the new one," a confederation spokesman told Reuters. "We will announce tomorrow how we will campaign against the new law."
The tough labour laws had drawn fire from human rights groups and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) which South Korea joined last year.
OECD chief Donald Johnston said on Monday that the December labour law was seen as inadequate by many OECD members.
He said South Korea was more likely to bring its labour into line with international norms as a member of the OECD than it would on the outside.
There is no labour code in the OECD, a consensus organisation but Johnston added: "Members will not accept a country unless it establishes criteria..."

Employers gained modest victories with provisions upholding the principle of "no work, no pay" for strikers and introducing flexible working hours. The bill's original intention to help struggling companies stay afloat by allowing them to shed staff was compromised.

President Kim Young-sam was forced to send the law back to parliament after its forced passage unleashed industrial unrest. Ruling party members had pushed it through in a dawn session while opposition members slept.
Kim had insisted that a flexible labour market was essential to improve the country's industrial competitiveness and reduce a worrying trade deficit.
The ruling party and the opposition groups cobbled together a compromise on the bill, composed of four sections.

But at the last moment, opposition groups insisted they would only support the law if the ruling camp also agreed to revise another controversial law restoring powers to the domestic intelligence agency. The move delayed the adoption of the new law by eight hours.

The law on the Agency for National Security Planning, which once hounded political dissidents, was railroaded through parliament along with the labour law. The ruling camp agreed to revise it during the current session of parliament.
There was also squabbling over an opposition demand for parliamentary hearings into a loans scandal that has rocked the nation and hurt President Kim's "Mr Clean" image.
Once again, the ruling camp backed down and promised cooperation over the hearings. There is still debate over who should be summoned to the hearings, and whether the proceedings should be televised.
